entities.summary:
Diwali, the Hindu, Jain, Sikh, Buddhist, and South Asian festival of lights, has a rich history spanning multiple continents and centuries. 

 It originated in the Vedic period in Southeast Asia around 1500 BCE and has since evolved into a global phenomenon celebrated by over 1 billion people in more than 100 countries. Diwali was influenced by the ancient Indian tradition of worshiping the goddess Lakshmi, who was associated with wealth, prosperity, and good fortune. The festival has undergone numerous transformations over the centuries, adapting to the changing social, cultural, and economic conditions of the regions in which it was celebrated. 

 Today, Diwali is celebrated on different dates in different parts of the world, with varying rituals and customs. In India, it is celebrated over five days, with each day having its own significance and significance. The festival is a symbol of the triumph of light over darkness, good over evil, and knowledge over ignorance. 

 As the festival continues to evolve and spread, it has become an integral part of the cultural heritage of the countries in which it is celebrated, leaving a lasting impact on the social, economic, and cultural landscape of the regions.
